en: I have longed for you.
Amid nothing but humiliation and misery,
I have burned for twelve years,
Thinking you would come alone.
“If my orphan should arrive,
He will overcome all whom he faces;
He will loosen one shackle
From this wretch who suffered grievously.
He will make the cruel flee;
He will cut off the enemy’s head,
Make splendid havoc in the slaughter,
And crush the cruel, formidable foe
To take his vengeance.”
So I have waited for you.
My poor head, which drank no kumis,
Thirsted even for muddy water.
When the magnanimous hero’s eyes closed,
Everything ended, and I became like snow.
When the noble gray-maned hero lived,
This head, which drank no liquor,
Thirsted for sour drink.
When my gray-maned uncle lived,
He bestowed good fortune.
Into my mouth, where no millet grain could fit,
A yearling calf’s head fitted with ease.
My panther uncle, the thoroughbred,
Sacked Bukhara and bestowed good fortune.
After my thoroughbred uncle passed away,
Into my mouth, where no grain of wheat could fit,
Even a bull’s head fitted with ease.
Every beating I saw became poison;
Everything I ate became a knucklebone.
My vigor failed and my strength departed;
From your laughing uncle, the mighty hero,
My power ebbed and my blood drained away.
What befell me was an iron cage;
What I endured was toil and misery;
What befell me was a deep pit.
Now that my brave orphan has come,
My ancient pain has stirred again.
Now that my extinguished fire has kindled,
Now that God has granted my destiny,
Now that what I prayed for has arrived,
Let me open the darkness to the light,
Let me calm my fevered heart,
And open wide my dimmed eyes.
My hero, cut down by calamity,
My champion left by the precious one,
My majesty left by the noble one,
My courage that marches before me,
My spring flowing close at hand,
Quenching my thirst when I am parched,
My champion beneath the planted banner,
My sturdy boy turning gray and white,
They adorned him with a black plume,
And tended Choro like a young child,
Wrapping him in layers of rich fat.
With every kind of healing medicine,
They dressed his wounds again and again,
Until his whole body began to move
And strength entered him.
A hundred times more than before,
His strength returned;
Fivefold beyond his former state,
Külchoro, upheld by the sacred spirit,
Came back to life.
His strength was restored anew;
There was no enemy left to fight.
Rampaging and slashing in his frenzy,
Your lion Choro surged with ardor
And regained his might.
Broad-backed and bracing himself,
He swayed as though struck from this side;
His bulk was like a ridge’s crest,
His surge like a raging flood.
If you looked upon his courage,
It was like the flame above a mountain valley;
His bullet-proof fists were like great knobs.
Such was the appearance
Of spirit-favored Külchoro.
The sable cap worn upon the head—
Who has not donned it with a flourish?
When fortune stood beside him,
Who did not stride about like thunder?
At the sight of the panther hero,
What enemy did not flee in panic?
He wore armor of blue steel;
Your gray-maned hero struck the foe once,
Then fitted his sword into its sheath.
Any enemy who met this wretch
Blessed by the holy wanderer fell.
When he rode, dust arose;
When he entered battle, blood flowed.
For twelve years, this ill-fated Choro
Endured his fate:
Carrying firewood upon his back,
Beaten by honorable men,
And abused by godless dogs,
I burned and hardened in the flames.
Thinking, “If he lives, he will be my shelter;
He will devour the many foes,
Make splendid havoc in the slaughter,
And take vengeance on the enemy,”
I burned with longing for you.
My broken wing has mended,
My only happiness has found me,
My grieving thoughts have faded,
And my tail has grown an armspan long.
Now that the hour of vengeance has come,
Every calamity has been cut away;
My sorrow has fled and I have recovered,
And once again grown mighty.
I received a letter from Kyzylsart,
And together we received Kyzыр’s blessing;
From my precious sister-in-law Chürök
I received a horse no bullet could catch.
After quietly washing away my filth,
From my fierce, tempestuous sister-in-law
I donned a coat no bullet could pierce.
My wasted strength grew full again,
My hungry belly was filled;
For me to eat, a barren mare
Was slaughtered when my orphan arrived.
My foster father Kyzylsart
Appeared with forty caravans,
And now the honor of sorrowing,
Afflicted Choro has been restored.
If sent ahead, his path is white;
If following behind, his army is countless.
The orphan named in the testament has been found,
And thus the honor of Choro,
Born for grief, has been restored.
Its shaft is sound and its tip is sharp—
The hollow-shafted ornamented spear.
I would increase my feats each time;
Setting hoes in a row,
I would shoot them with my bow.
My arrow would be blunted,
And the faces of the hoes gouged in.
I girded on crimson steel,
And precious Khan Bakai tested me,
Saying, “His strength will suffice for the world.”
Thinking, “He will become someone’s spokesman,”
My dear mother Kanykei
Had me raised with sacred rites.
“The strength of this wrestler is unique,”
Said the saint who led the people,
The collar of the precious robe,
The father of the peoples of the age,
The elder sustained by the sacred spirit,
The sage who had seen many lands—
My uncle Koshoy approved of me.
“Choro’s valor is great and his strength supreme,
Though he is unruly,”
Said heroic Koshoy, approving me when he saw me.
My prowess became known;
“He is a fearsome warrior,” they said,
And when they saw my courage,
Many heroes despaired of their lives.
Wondering whether I was the greater warrior,
Our grandfather Chylaba
Questioned a sorcerer.
When he heard that I was a hero,
He was astonished and amazed.
Lo Ma, the khan of Beijing,
Heard that my valor was exceptional,
And my strength beyond measure;
As the son of Khan Almambet,
My fame became known among the people.
I loaded the great musket,
And only the hardest part
Of the unyielding black earth stopped its shot.
Where I stood became a fortress;
Every enemy I met became a fool.
Life burst from his breastbone.
Such was his prowess:
He played with his ornamented spear,
And every enemy he met crawled away.
He was a hero of surpassing stature,
A panther, a gray-maned warrior—
Such was Külchoro.
Brimming with strength and spreading broad,
Your hero Choro, attended by the sacred spirit,
Your Choro, a hero surpassing the world,
Whose thoroughbred could carry him for six months,
Kinsman of the magnanimous khan—
He too was one of the greatest.
Would the lion-like gray-maned hero stay still?
He summoned Kyzylsart, Seytek, and the Black Giant,
The three of them, to the spectacle;
Would he refrain from wreaking havoc?
He summoned up his former strength.
When the sword Zulpukor
Hung from my arm,
When I wore trousers
That no bullet could pierce,
When I crushed the whole wide world
And held it in my power,
When the hungry blade Achalbars
Swung from my arm,
When I crushed the whole wide world
And took possession of it,
When I brought disaster upon any foe
Who crossed my path,
When I destroyed everyone I encountered
And seized all before me,
All twelve parts of my body were whole.
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
A full-limbed, bold young warrior,
I made much blood flow across the plains;
Such was my stony courage and strength.
While my sovereign lived,
While I possessed my former strength,
Among all humankind,
He loaded the white musket.
From the hero’s fury,
The black earth, whose breast is hairy,
Stopped the shot only in its deepest layers.
When he raged in wrath,
The whole wide world stood watch;
The thick black earth below
Smoldered through its deepest layers
From my khan uncle’s fury.
When the providential hero lived,
Crimson steel took heads;
Against whoever provoked his wrath,
He ravaged the world and set it aflame.
He kindled the grassy lands
And set the meadows afire.
My exceedingly noble sultan uncle
Was truly a hero;
Among all humankind,
That peerless, keen-eyed eagle
Was truly a lion.
He broke through dead ends and opened roads;
My falcon uncle, my eagle,
Broke through on every side and opened roads,
And struck down all who opposed him.
He swept aside everyone he met,
And burned everyone he encountered.
Along the great road no host could overtake,
He made his bay horse dance;
Subduing everyone he encountered,
He made his assailants crawl.
He broke fortresses and took khans;
Against innumerable foes,
He raised dust such as no man had seen.
At the hero’s fury,
The enemies who grappled with him stood amazed.
When his fit of rage seized him,
He fiercely launched the turmoil.
He cut off the heads
Of the enemies who attacked him and subdued them;
He was truly a mighty mainstay.

Along broad Talas,
